newsitem.title: USA: NYC watchdog sees growth slowing to 1.5 pct in '97.
newsitem.headline: NYC watchdog sees growth slowing to 1.5 pct in '97.

text.p: The New York City comptroller on Monday forecast that the city's economy would slow to 1.5 percent growth in 1997, down from 1.8 percent in 1996, and urged the Giuliani Admnistration to refocus its efforts on small business.
The comptroller, a Democrat who decided not to run against Republican Mayor Rudolph Giuliani in next year's race, also criticized the mayor for waffling over some tax cuts.

"Uncertainity is a deterrent to sustainable investment. It is important for the city not to raise expectations about tax cuts and then fail to deliver," he wrote in the report, mandated by the city charter.
As examples, he cited a pledge to repeal the 12.5 percent personal income tax surcharge and the sales tax on items of clothing that cost less than $100.

Hevesi added Giuliani had given too much weight to keeping large businesses in New York City by giving them tax breaks and other incentives. "The city's economic development activity should refocus more of its effort on small businesses, the only source of new jobs in the 1990s."

Despite the strong rebound on Wall Street, the city comptroller looked for tax revenues to gain $10 million less than the Giuliani Administration, which forecast tax revenues would rise $450 million in fiscal year 1997. Hevesi said his office was less optimistic about real property and commercial rent taxes but more bullish on the business and sales taxes.

The downturn in the city's inflation-adjusted gross city products was partly due to a fall in local retail sales, which slowed to a 1.3 percent expansion in the third quarter, down from the 4.1 percent growth seen in the first half. Job gains in the private sector fell to 1,200 jobs a month since June, down from the 4,700 pace of additions seen in the first half.
Other highlights of the comptroller's report follow.

--New York City's economy grew more slowly than the nation's, which rose 2.2 percent in the third quarter, and other large cities. City employment rose 0.7 percent in the first nine months of 1996, the sixth lowest among 15 cities, while its jobless rate, at 8.6 percent was the highest.

--Employment was predicted to rise by 20,000 jobs in 1997 by Hevesi, down slightly from 24,000 in 1996, as losses in the public sector should help offset private hiring, leaving the jobless rate hovering around 8.6 percent.
--Big year-end bonuses paid by Wall Street financial companies could help boost the city wage rate 5.9 percent in 1997.
--The New York area consmuer price index will rise 2.8 percent in 1997, down from three percent in 1996.
